                                    SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
                                       PUC DOCKET NO. 59475


JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR                                   §            BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE
ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC                                §
AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES                               §                                OF
CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR                                   §

AND NECESSITY FOR THE BELL                                   §
COUNTY EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL                               §
SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION                               §
LINE PROJECT IN BELL BURNET,                                 §
CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS,                                   §

WILLIAMSON COUNTIES

           JG & WILSON SISTERS RANCH, LTD. INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

           COMES NOW JG & Wilson Sisters Ranch, Ltd., in the above-styled case, and pursuant to

SOAH Order No. 19, 1 files this Initial Post-Hearing Brief and would like to show the following:

                                   INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

           JG & Wilson Sisters Ranch, Ltd. submit this Initial Post-Hearing Brief in Docket No.

59475 in opposition of any route utilizing in order of priority Link J24 and Link J27 and in support

of any route not utilizing Link J24 and Link J27, e.g., Route 487, the route selected by the Public

Utility Commission (“PUC”), best satisfies PURA and the Commission’s routing criteria. 2

                                                 ARGUMENT

           Routes that do not utilize Link J24 and Link J27 best meet routing criteria.



1
    SOAH Order No. 32 at 2, PUC No. 59475 H’rg (filed on the Interchange on Jun. 15, 2026).
2
 See Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. No. 23, PUC No. 59475 H’rg (providing the route ID & link sequence description for
potential routes).




{1753/008/00308852.DOCX;2 }                              1
           Both Applicant and PUC’s recommended routes mirror each other from the Bell County

East substation west to the Link J10/H1 node, then split with the PUC’s recommended route going

to the north along Links J10, J11, J12, and J13 and Applicant’s preferred route going to the south

along Links H1, H41, H42, J21, J22, J23, J27, and J4, before reconnecting at the Link J13/J4 node

to continue west along identical links for over forty (40) miles through San Saba and McCulloch

Counties, Texas before splitting again at the Link M12/M7 node and then coming together a final

time at the N3/O3/P2/01 node to resume their identical course west to the Big Hill Substation. 3

This brief will focus on the distinction between the PUC and Applicant’s recommended routes

between the Link J10/H1 node and the Link J13/J4 node (“Eastern Split”).

          The use of Routes which include Link J24 and Link J27 are a far more burdensome

approach to achieving the primary objective of the project. Under Section 25.101 of the Texas

Administrative Code, “[a]n application for a new transmission line must address the criteria in

PURA §37.056(c) and considering those criteria, engineering constraints, and costs, the line must

be routed to the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected community and

landowners.” 4 The use of Link J11 or other more northern links that are superior in cost, length,

engineering constraints and minimize agricultural impact and visibility best accomplish these

considerations. 5

          Cost.

          For the Eastern Split, utilizing the PUC’s Route 487 is $9 million less expensive than

whole, the factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and in 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).”).

{1753/008/00308852.DOCX;2 }                            2
 Applicant’s Route 894. 6 Routing the transmission line south to the H Links alone triples the length

and adds at least $7 million in cost. 7 Oncor’s Transmission Engineering Manager Corin E. Cooley

testified that, “[g]enerally, the larger the angle, the greater the associated cost.” 8 Later during cross-

examination, she further acknowledged that, although other factors such as overall line length and

location also influence cost, “adding turning locations does increase cost.” 9 The PUC’s Eastern

Split has only 14 angles on four links compared to Applicant’s Eastern Split having 26 angles on

eight links. For Link J22 on the Applicant’s Eastern Split, at least three hard angles are required to

cross the Colorado River and the accompanying sensitive riparian areas. 10 Whereas the PUC’s

Eastern Split crossing of the Colorado on Link J11 does not require any hard angles. 11 The PUC’s

Eastern Split is also 9.2% shorter than Applicant’s Eastern Split. 12 Increases in distance from these

additional links—when applied across large-scale transmission projects—compound into

substantially greater land use, environmental disturbance, and long-term operational impact across

a multiplied number of affected property owners.

           The cost estimates for the Applicant’s proposed alternative routes cannot be guaranteed.

The cost estimates not only inherently include a contingency that may result in increases of

approximately 10–15%, 13 but the Applicant’s analysis and recommendations fail to account for

increased cost due to environmental factors, an analysis which has not been started. 14 When asked

 about such concerns, the Applicant states that they will “work” with landowners, or that these sorts

of costs “contribute to the estimated cost for each transmission line route.” 15 Ms. Cooley testified

that, “the study area does not contain any known engineering constraints that cannot be resolved

with additional consideration during the design and construction phases.” 16 The Applicant’s belief

that every cost that may arise is blanketed into the estimate or can be worked out with the

landowner is a work of fiction. 17 What she neglects to mention, is that those constraints not only

increase the cost, but that the design and construction phases happen after a route is chosen 18—

meaning that if such concerns arise, the cost increase was not originally accounted for. For

example, the Applicants Eastern Split includes Link J4, which after landowner input, the

Applicants have already had to modify “to avoid placement of a transmission line turn and

associated structures on steep terrain.” 19

professionals such as Vegetation Management Contractors, 20 Qualified Biologists, 21 Biological

Monitor, 22 Qualified Geologists, 23 Qualified Geotechnical Engineers, 24 Qualified Cultural

            The lack of cost accountability in the estimate goes further than environmental-related

concerns alone as a vast majority of critical project design infrastructure such as, “[t]he exact

numbers and types of tower structures are not known at this time and will be determined.” 28 For

reserved production slots for large power transformers, shunt reactors, and circuit breakers by the

Applicant, Applicant objected to answering if the Applicant’s cost estimate assumes that slots will

be available at current pricing when procurement is initiated. 29 This uncertainty on the cost is

exactly what the U.S. Department of Energy has made clear; “[c]ontingency is not to be used to

avoid making an accurate assessment of expected cost.” 30 Route 894’s already extravagant cost

includes specifically a higher cost for procurement of materials and equipment. 31

            The concerns raised by the use of Link J11 have already been disproven. 32 The location of

the existing flood control structures are known and as such were considered during route

development resulting in the transmission line being routed around the Lampasas County water

impoundment. 33 Russell Marusak for the Applicant assured the ALJs and Intervenors that the

proposed transmission line will not impact the single flood control structure in proximity to Link

           The Applicant’s Eastern split, besides bringing forth a greater cost and environmental

impact, has a larger impact on the livelihood of the landowner it will affect. Greater than 68%

percent of Applicant’s Eastern Split includes agriculturally impacted land, including cropland, hay

meadow, rangeland pasture, and cropland with mobile irrigation systems. 36 In contract, the PUC’s

Eastern Split’s impact on agricultural land is less than half that. The Applicant’s Eastern split also

has over 44% more stream crossings than the PUC’s Eastern Split. 37 Furthermore, the PUC’s

Eastern Split has less length across commercial/industrial areas, wetlands, known habitat of

federally listed endangered/threated species, high archeological/historical site potential, and FAA-

registered airports within 10,000 feet, 38 thus reducing engineering constraints pertaining to

existing structures, bodies of water, runways, and geological features as well as the impact on

views long-established agricultural land use practices, rural income, sustainability, and

generational ownership of agricultural land. 39 Selecting Route 897, an already more expensive

option and an option the Applicant’s themselves have not denied will likely incur additional

unforeseen construction-related costs, 40 does not represent a prudent or responsible course of

action.

           Route 487 best satisfies the Commission’s routing criteria.

           The PUC’s Eastern Split is a record-supported superior route to routes that utilize Link J24

or Link J27. Route 487 adheres to the principle that a route must be supported by evidence of cost,

feasibility, and its effect on the routing criteria under PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101. 41 The

record reaffirms how Route 487 preserves Route 894’s most favorable attributes while removing

the issues created by the inclusion of Link J27 and replacing it with Links J11 and J12’s superior

corridor utilization, reduced fragmentation, avoidable impacts to ranch infrastructure and water

resources, all while maintaining engineering feasibility and lowering cost by $16.1 million. 42

          At 221.5 miles, Route 487 is only 7.1 miles longer and 1.7% more costly than the shortest

and least expensive routes. 43 Furthermore, Route 487 has the lowest length in proximity to parks

recreational areas, agricultural cropland with mobile irrigation systems, woodlands, cropland,

rangeland, streams, habitats of federally listed endangered or threated species, areas of

archaeological and historical significance, commercial/industrial areas, private airstrips, FAA-

registered airports within 10,000 feet, heliports, and commercial AM radio transmitters. 44 Route

487 has a greater milage paralleling existing compatible rights-of-way than does Applicant’s Route

894—which aids in reducing costs, is better for the landowner, and was a recommendation that

Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) suggested to minimize habitat fragmentation. 45

Route 487 itself materially improves compatible corridor utilization while simultaneously

reducing fragmentation impacts and maintaining manageable cost differences. Route 894’s higher

           Route selection analysis requires a careful balancing of all considerations in PURA and the

Commission rules, “not simply counting which route performs best in the most individual

metrics.” 48 Accordingly, significant weight should not be placed on the fact that Route 894

performs greater as to habitable structures, as the difference is only 11% and the performance of

Route 487 remains overall superior. The Applicant’s witnesses have made it clear that although

habitable structures are considered, “[t]his does not mean that a proposed transmission line must

avoid habitable structures at all costs, but that reasonable alternatives should be considered.” 49

           Oncor’s CNN Project Specialist, Casey Petty, recommended that “the Commission

consider the 121 additional alternative routes” not just the Applicant’s preferred Route 894. 50

Additionally, Ms. Perkins testified that “all 122 filed routes are acceptable,” and that “it’s up to

the Commission to consider which route they deem considering all the factors.” 51 Route 487 was

also included on the Applicant’s routes of interest map. 52 John Poole concluded that the

Commission deems Route 487 to be the best route when “weighing, as a whole, the factors set

           Given these considerations, with its lower projected costs and more robust Environmental

Assessment data, Route 487 stands out as the more prudent and well-substantiated option.

           JG & Wilson Sisters Ranch, Ltd. oppose any routes utilizing Link J24 or Link J27.

           JG & Wilson Sisters Ranch, Ltd. oppose any route utilizing Link J24 or Link J27, because

of their significant impact to the JG & Wilson Sisters Ranch, Ltd.’s unique riparian property.

           A transmission line built on Link J24 or Link J27 would bisect JG & Wilson Sisters Ranch,

Ltd.’s properties, adversely impacting not only the farming and ranching operations, but causing

such significant damage as to transform the very topographical diversity that gives the property its

environmental significance. 55 The unique convergence of fragile limestone uplands, dropping off

to riparian bottomlands, feeding into spring fed creeks is what allows JG & Wilson Sisters Ranch,

Ltd. to sustain the livestock and wildlife operations that form a crucial ecological pillar of

 Cherokee Creek, a diverse waterway that hosts protected migratory birds and archaeological

           For farming operations, the Applicant’s assertion that impacts are “season-dependent” does

not demonstrate mitigation. 57 The suggestion that construction impacts to harvesting crops is

dependent on the season ignores the reality that modern agricultural operations require continuous,

large-scale equipment use throughout the year. 58 Even if construction occurs outside harvest, it

interferes with planting, cultivation, and field maintenance—each of which is essential to the JG

& Wilson Sisters Ranch, Ltd.’s productivity. Instead, it confirms that the Project will impose

unavoidable and recurring disruptions across all phases of agricultural operations. Given the scale

of the Project and the number of affected properties, the Applicant cannot realistically coordinate

construction in a manner that avoids material interference with agricultural operations. 59 Instead,

the Project poses a sustained and material threat to the livelihood of the JG & Wilson Sisters Ranch,

Ltd. that cannot be meaningfully minimized through scheduling. 60 Construction on Link J24 or

Link J27 does not merely inconvenience JG & Wilson Sisters Ranch, Ltd.; it directly impairs the

productive capacity of the land, which is the basis of the landowner’s livelihood.

            The Applicant acknowledges that “there will be temporary interruption within the ROW

during construction,” which in itself poses a serious risk for operations that rely on open pasture

and require uninterrupted grazing patterns. 61 The construction of such wide easements reduces the

amount of usable grazing land and disrupts pasture layouts, making it more difficult to manage

livestock. Heavy equipment used during installation will compact soil, damage vegetation, and

disturb water drainage patterns, affecting forage quality.

           Additionally, the terrain found on Link J24 and Link J27 is not adequate for constructing

and maintaining transmission lines. 62 Constructing transmission lines across porous limestone

caverns that support a diverse ecosystem is both environmentally disruptive and ecologically

irresponsible. The landscapes along Links J24 and J27 provide critical habitat for sensitive species,

including bald eagles, whose nesting and hunting patterns depend on undisturbed surroundings

and tall natural vantage points. 63 The installation process—requiring clearing and heavy

equipment— fragment habitats and introduces long-term disturbances that threaten local

biodiversity. The presence of large transmission structures and power lines increases the risk of

collisions and electrocution for birds, directly endangering populations that are already carefully

 managed. The Applicant’s proposal to relocate bald eagles and other migratory birds is not a valid

or effective management strategy. 64 Due to their strong site fidelity, territorial behavior, and legal

protections, these species cannot be successfully displaced without significant risk of harm or

displacement-related impacts. For these reasons, the environmentally sensitive and wildlife-rich

areas found along Link J24 and Link J27 are fundamentally unsuitable locations for transmission

line development, and routes that avoid Link J24 and Link J27 should be prioritized.

          Link J24 and Link J27 do not parallel existing transmission lines across the JG & Wilson

Sisters Ranch, Ltd. Rather, the extensive footprint of proposed lattice towers through JG & Wilson

Sisters Ranch, Ltd., boxes in the ranch with existing transmission lines making it unsafe to operate

equipment and detrimental to the agricultural, wildlife, and conservation purposes of the ranch.

                                             CONCLUSION

                   JG & Wilson Sisters Ranch, Ltd., submits this Initial Post-Hearing Brief in Docket

No. 59475 in strong opposition to any route that, in order of priority, utilizes Link J24 or Link J27,

to include Applicant’s preferred Route 894. JG & Wilson Sisters Ranch, Ltd., supports any Route

that does not utilize Link J24 or Link J27, e.g., the PUC’s recommended Route 487. The record

does not support that Route 894 provides superior overall balancing of the Commission’s routing

criteria relative to Route 487. Importantly, Route 487 achieves these improvements while

remaining identical to Route 894 across approximately 60% of the Project. Route 487 preserves

much of Route 894’s broader framework while materially improving compatible corridor

utilization and reducing fragmentation impacts across the eastern portion of the Project. JG &

Wilson Sisters Ranch, Ltd. requests the Administrative Law Judges recommend any route that

does not, in order of priority, utilize Link J24 or Link J27.

the issues created by the inclusion of Link J27 and replacing it with Links Jl 1 and J12's superior

corridor utilization, reduced fragmentation, avoidable impacts to ranch infrastructure and water

resources, all while maintaining engineering feasibility and lowering cost by $16.1 million.42

rangeland, streams, habitats of federally listed endangered or threated species, areas of

archaeological and historical significance, commercial/industrial areas, private airstrips, FAA-

registered airports within 10,000 feet, heliports, and commercial AM radio transmitters. 44 Route

487 has a greater milage paralleling existing compatible rights-of-way than does Applicant's Route

894-which aids in reducing costs, is better for the landowner, and was a recommendation that

Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) suggested to minimize habitat fragmentation. 45

Route 487 itself materially improves compatible corridor utilization while simultaneously

reducing fragmentation impacts and maintaining manageable cost differences. Route 894' s higher
